newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street embraces Rubin, but dlr doubts persist.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street embraces Rubin, but dlr doubts persist.

text.p: Expectation that U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will stay on the job and continue to back a strong dollar reassured Wall Street, but doubts persist about the U.S. currency's future direction, experts said.
"Rubin has done an outstanding job in tackling some of the issues," said Dimitri Balatsos, president of Tesseract Partners Inc, an investment management firm.
"However, there is only so much any administration, any Secretary of the Treasury, any central bank can (do to) influence the direction of a currency with words," he added.

Balatsos emphasized that economic fundamentals ultimately determine the direction of a currency. Furthermore, Fed actions on interest rates are more important than any arm twisting or dollar jawboning by the Treasury.
Since Rubin took over the helm of the Treasury, Wall Street has become well acquainted with his mantra: a strong dollar is in the U.S.'s best interest.
Just two days after President Bill Clinton won re-election on Tuesday, many top cabinet officials have already made plans to resign. Yet there has been no official word on Rubin's plans.
A source close to Rubin told Reuters Wednesday the Secretary was expected to remain on the job. Some analysts are betting that means Rubin will stay the dollar-policy course.

"He's made it clear that he believes the strength in the stock market, the lower level of interest rates and inflation are a function of a strong dollar," said Tim McGee, chief economist at Tokai Bank Ltd. "It's very unlikely that that policy is going to change."
McGee said the administration's position on the dollar will not likely change unless there is a period of economic weakness.

National Association of Manufacturers' President Jerry Jasinowski also told reporters Thursday that Rubin will be saying less about the strong dollar as the economy slows but he does not expect Rubin to start talking the dollar down.
Under Rubin, the dollar has battled back from a post World War II low of 79.75 yen reached on April 19, 1995 to 114.92 yen hit on October 29 this year.

Wall Street also took note that Nikkei Financial Daily quoted the Director General of the International Finance Bureau of Japan's Finance Ministry, saying the dollar rebound from 1995's sharp slide versus the yen was about to end.
Nikkei Financial also quoted Eisuke Sakakibara as saying the ministry was not trying to push the yen down further.

"People are taking it seriously because the timing is very important ... the day after the U.S. election," McGee of Tokai said. "It may be that there's some tacit input from the U.S. that maybe they don't want the yen to keep getting weaker so fast," he added.
Remarks from Jasinowski and Sakakibara pressured the dollar on Thursday, which traded at 111.40/50 yen just after midday, well below 113.92/02 at Wednesday's close.
The dollar's sell-off on Thursday was welcomed by some market participants who played down the importance of Sakakibara's remarks.

"Whether or not the Japanese finance ministry thinks that the yen is too weak at 115, 114 or 113 level is immaterial," said John Krey, a vice president and chief investment strategist at Barclays Private Bank.
Krey emphasized the Japanese economy needs a weak yen to promote growth.
He deemed the sell-off on Thursday as a good buying opportunity and predicted the dollar could rally to 116 or 117 yen by the end of the year.
